So the OnReset ApplyTime should be supported for all VRs, correct? As shown in [1], both Immediate and OnReset are currently handled. I think we should raise a separate patch to restrict ApplyTime support to OnReset only in I2CVRSoftwareManager.

[1] https://grok.openbmc.org/xref/openbmc/phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt/i2c-vr/i2cvr_software_manager.cpp?r=466c66a3df6b295b851094480fd5513d790cfa67&mo=3060&fi=93#93

@paligill@gmail.com For ISL69269 and XDPE1X2XX VRs, a reset command is available to let the VR take affect (CC @christopher.meis@9elements.com). However, MPS VRs don't support such a reset command. Therefore, restricting ApplyTime support to OnReset may not be appropriate for all VR types.
This is correct. Some VRs do need a reset, some dont.

Why NOLInt?

The NOLINT directive is used because the Clang analyzer repeatedly reports `Branch condition evaluates to a garbage value`. This warning likely results from passing the crc variable as a pointer to the overridden getCRC(uint32_t* checksum) function, which causes the analyzer to incorrectly assume it may be uninitialized.
This kind of error occured in the other VR implementations as well. I still haven't figured out how to solve it. We agreed on keeping the NOLINT in such cases.

Why true? Shouldn't this be false instead?

The reset() function is called by the parent I2CVRDevice::updateDevice(). If it returns false, the update process is considered a failure (see [1]). However, since MPS VRs do not support a reset command, this implementation simply returns true.

Why is this specific to MPS? How does other VRs handle this?

Other VR implementations define control commands as constexpr uint8_t rather than using enum class, so they don’t need to explicitly static_cast to uint8_t. However, using enum class improves type safety and clarity, which I believe is the better approach.

To simplify the code and avoid repetitive casting, I replaced the original writeData() function with a more general buildByteVector() utility. This function constructs a std::vector<uint8_t> from a flexible set of arguments, including enums, integral types, and initializer lists, making it easier to assemble byte packets or command sequences in a consistent and readable way.
